items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Companies are charging ahead with AI—even though middle managers are not ready for it
items.content_html:
As Joelle Emerson has watched companies cull the ranks of middle management and pour resources into AI, there has been one key question on her mind: What role is the chief people officer playing in that shift? 

“I think chief people officers should be leaders in the transformation [that] organizations are undergoing right now with AI,” says Emerson, the cofounder and CEO of culture and inclusion platform Paradigm. “I see a lot of companies making a lot of changes very, very quickly—for example, collapsing management layers.”

“It makes me wonder where the chief people officer is in some of those conversations,” she continues. “It seems likely to me that those organizations, or at least some of them, are going to struggle with actually getting people to change in the ways that are required right now.” 

In a new survey of HR leaders from over 650 companies, Paradigm sought to better understand how companies are evolving and where they might be getting in their own way, in part because they are not fully empowering leaders who oversee people and culture functions. 

Paradigm’s analysis found that across a breadth of industries—be it tech, financial services, retail, or healthcare—employers are confronting some of the same challenges. Over half of the companies said ramping up AI adoption was a core priority, while 75% of them cited operational efficiency. 

But many employers appear to be falling short of those aspirations. According to Paradigm’s report, companies have limited faith in their managers even as they trim head count and expect them to do more with less. When asked whether their managers are ready to lead through change, only a fraction of HR leaders said their managers were adequately prepared; three-quarters of respondents said their managers were either unprepared or only prepared in some functions. 

While many companies were taking steps to train their managers, providing coaching and other resources, they were not necessarily addressing a broader issue—that managers simply had too much on their plate. 

“I think no matter what organization you’re in or what your philosophy is on the future of org structure, what is definitely true is that companies are asking managers to do more than ever,” Emerson says. As Fast Company has reported, middle managers are taking on more and more as their employers demand broader AI adoption. 

That can mean overseeing more direct reports, being responsible for them adopting AI, or reviewing the output as employees produce work more quickly with AI. Emerson points out that there could be an opportunity here for corporate leaders—namely chief people officers—to message AI adoption differently, framing it as a way for managers to focus on the more human aspects of their job. 

“Almost everything we found in [this study] is sort of validating this concern I have that there’s so much exciting opportunity, but we’re not seeing it fulfilled,” Emerson says. “I think the HR function has so much potential right now to flip that and say we’re going to be empowering managers; we’re going to be telling a different story.”

Another trend the study highlights is that there’s a significant gap between what companies want to achieve with artificial intelligence and how successfully they are implementing it. Over a third of the leaders polled by Paradigm admitted AI was largely used in a more experimental way, while 38% claimed it was only implemented in certain workflows. At a number of companies, the results of AI pilots and experimentation were not shared across the entire organization. 

“I actually think there’s a lot of good that comes from letting people experiment with tools and figure out what works,” Emerson says. “It is pretty useless if you have everyone doing that in isolation and not sharing with one another what they’re learning.” 

The report captures a paradox that Emerson believes is standing in the way of companies truly reaping the benefits of AI adoption: Over 30% of the companies surveyed, for example, had not employed AI for HR functions—even as chief people officers and other HR leaders are being tasked with leading organizations through this moment. In fact, only a third of leaders said they were very confident their company could radically change how work gets done by using AI, beyond simply giving employees new tools to use. 

Paradigm’s findings suggest that even HR leaders are somewhat skeptical about what their company can actually accomplish with AI. But Emerson claims there is hope if employers enable them to take the lead and bring them into strategy discussions, rather than overlooking leaders who oversee people and culture. 

“Chief people officers have always been advocating for their seat at the strategy table,” Emerson says. “We’re in a phase of transformation now that is more significantly about human behavior. And if you realize that’s the case, fundamentally you have to have someone in the driver’s seat who knows about those things.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Flock adds platform guardrails after misuse and privacy concerns spark backlash
items.content_html:
Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company increasingly under scrutiny from lawmakers from both parties, civil liberties advocates, and citizens across the U.S., announced Thursday that it is making changes to its platform intended to quell privacy concerns and address documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.

The company operates a vast nationwide network of automated cameras that record the license plate numbers and other characteristics of all passing vehicles every day. Thousands of law enforcement agencies in 49 states can search and share Flock’s data across jurisdictions to aid their investigations.

Police have credited the technology as an important crime-fighting innovation that has helped locate missing people and track suspects in violent crimes. But some critics say its pervasiveness amounts to unconstitutional warrantless mass surveillance. Dozens of cities and agencies have nixed their relationships with Flock amid concerns that the data can be accessed for immigration enforcement or used in unauthorized tracking, after a flurry of examples surfaced of law enforcement officers misusing the technology for personal searches.

CEO says changes will drive accountability

In an interview, Flock CEO Garrett Langley said many of the product changes will make what were once optional guardrails mandatory for its users to implement by January 1.

Among them: All law enforcement customers will have to implement an audit tool that’s intended to flag abnormal search behavior. When the system detects abnormal behavior, the user would be locked out pending an internal review, the company said in a description of the changes provided ahead of Thursday’s announcement.

Flock, which says its customers own the data that the cameras record, is also shortening the standard data retention window from 30 days to seven. It said it will allow data to be preserved for longer when it is evidence tied to a case number.

Law enforcement users will now also be required to enter a code from their records management system tying each search to a specific case before it is run, something Langley said civil liberties advocates have long been calling for. Overrides for emergencies would be automatically flagged for review, the company said.

Customers will also be allowed to decide which offense types—such as homicide or arson—outside agencies can search their data for, which would allow a customer to block outside searches related to immigration enforcement, the company said.

Langley said that change will give individual cities and departments control to use the system in a manner “consistent with community values.”

Critics say updates still leave room for abuses, supporters urge balance

Critics of the company reacted skeptically to the changes, which they said appeared designed to address the growing bipartisan anger about the cameras but could still leave room for police to abuse the system.

The American Civil Liberties Union said in a blog post that the shortened evidence retention window could be “a step in the right direction,” but it characterized the other changes as “retreads” of inadequate safety measures.

Robert Frommer, a senior attorney at the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm that’s led closely watched litigation over the technology, called the changes “window dressing” from a company in “panic mode.”

“This is window dressing that doesn’t address the fundamental problem, which is that police officers are the ones deciding who and when to search, and that should be done by judges with real warrants,” he said.

Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a professor at the George Washington University Law School whose scholarship has focused on policing, big data surveillance, and the Fourth Amendment, said Thursday’s shifts were “better than the opposite” but called for further scrutiny of the technology in the form of “sustained democratic engagement with the rules and judicial checks on access at a minimum.”

Ferguson said he’s been surprised to see the “growing community backlash” against Flock specifically, given that the technology isn’t new and other companies sell it as well. But Flock and the movement against it have “captured people’s sense that maybe they don’t want to be surveilled all the time,” he said.

More than 50 agencies or jurisdictions have canceled, suspended, or rejected a contract, or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of the year, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a grassroots group formed to track the use of license plate reader technology and push back against it. Cameras around the country have also been vandalized.

In Congress, Republican representatives filed at least two bills aiming to restrict the use of the technology in July.

Ian Adams, an associate professor of criminology at the University of South Carolina currently working on a Flock-related research study, said many of the concerns raised about how the company’s data can be used are not new concerns in law enforcement.

“Anyone with policing experience could have reasonably foreseen that what have been termed as ‘curiosity searches’ by officers, searches for private reasons not related to police work, were going to be a problem this technology faced,” he added, noting that other technologies and platforms like the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information had faced those issues.

Law enforcement experts said it’s a common tension of “policing in a democracy”—balancing useful technology that officers say helps solve and prevent crime with the community’s interest and right to privacy.

“It’s a balancing act. A community has a legitimate interest in how information is used, but it also has a legitimate interest in the effectiveness of a police department in preventing crime,” said Chuck Wexler, executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, a Washington-based nonpartisan think tank. “I think a balance can be struck, but it’s more likely to come from department policy than company changes.”

Successes and failures have captured attention

Flock, based in Atlanta, Georgia, often posts to its website what the company deems to be everyday examples of success stories for its cameras, including finding missing seniors and catching car thieves. But the tech has also been used in high-profile cases that have garnered national attention, such as the search for a suspect in a fatal shooting at Brown University and in tracking and arresting a former North Carolina police officer who authorities say had made threats that he planned to carry out a mass shooting at a festival in Louisiana.

Abuses have also drawn widespread attention. The Washington Post reported earlier this month finding nearly 50 instances of police officers charged or accused of using the cameras for unauthorized purposes, many for tracking current or former romantic partners or family members.

Just this week, six employees—including four officers—of the Savannah Police Department in Georgia were fired after they were accused of searching for friends and family using the tool and allowing an officer from an outside agency to use the city’s cameras.

The Savannah department said it was made aware of the misuse through Flock’s voluntary audit function.

—By Sarah Rankin and Claudia Lauer, Associated Press

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] This school security system displays safe evacuation routes during shootings and disasters
items.content_html:
In the event of an emergency, evacuating a building can be one of the most important safety measures. But depending on the kind of emergency—whether a fire or a tornado or an active shooting—taking the right evacuation route or finding shelter can be the difference between life and death.

Go To Green is a new emergency evacuation system that’s designed to automatically direct people to go, or stay, in the safest place during an emergency. Designed primarily as a response to active shooter situations in schools, the system uses a simple system of colored lights to direct people to the safest evacuation route, and away from danger.

“Most children in the United States play red light, green light. So it just makes sense to use lights that we’re all preconditioned to pretty much from birth,” says Ernie Williams, founder of Go To Green.

The system consists of thin ceiling-mounted LED light arrays and various audio and motion sensors that activate at the sound of gunshots or during fires. Located in school hallways and inside and outside classroom doors, the lights turn green to show people where to move and red to show them where to avoid. Red and blue lights flash at the point nearest the emergency source, be it a fire or a shooter. It essentially turns buildings themselves into real-time evacuation tools, showing in a very visual way where to go during an emergency, and where not to.

Williams, a former Marine, spent 25 years in the military and says the idea for a more intuitive active-shooter security system and evacuation guide came from direct experience. “I spent a little bit of time getting shot at and understood the problem with indoor systems,” he says. “They can’t pick up an active shooter in real time.”

Williams says Go To Green’s sensors act independently to be able to pinpoint where a threat exists, even if it’s moving. “Let’s say a guy’s walking down the hallway and he shoots, the sensors change and the pathways may change,” he says.

The system is currently installed in 20 schools, mostly in Texas, where the company is based. None have been called into action for active shooter situations, but they have been activated during tornadoes, alerting students and staff to get indoors and avoid dangerous places within buildings. The company is backed by O’Leary Ventures, the investment arm of Shark Tank star Kevin O’Leary.

Primarily focused on active shooters, the security system is also designed to assist first responders, with exterior lights that flash blue and red to indicate the location of the threat, be it a fire or a person with a gun. “We can direct them using visual signals. We don’t have to get on the radios, we don’t have to get on the phone with them. They look up and see a visual and this automatically takes them to the threat,” Williams says.

Go To Green is one of many school security systems and tools that have come to market in recent years. Amanda Klinger, director of operations at the nonprofit security training organization The Educator’s School Safety Network, says products on the market vary widely in their efficacy. “We’ve really seen the industry explode in growth,” Klinger says. “There’s a lot of money to be made.”

After reviewing material on the Go To Green active-shooter security system, Klinger says it has the potential to be a valuable part of a school’s security system, but that security systems alone can only go so far. Training and threat prevention are also necessary to reduce the chances of very rare and extreme emergency events like active shooter situations. “The part that’s a little bit tough to swallow is, in a district where they opt for something like this, have they done appropriate training for their folks and for their students?” Klinger says. “Is this the icing on the cake, or is this the only thing that they’ve done?”

Klinger worries that school districts may dedicate limited resources to products and systems as seemingly simple solutions, without putting the same effort and resources into training and prevention. “The concern that we have with stuff like this, that does seem like a pretty good idea, that does seem to have a good amount of efficacy and utility, is does the school district then also have the political will to do some things on the other side of the coin?” Klinger says. “Because this is something that is only response. There is not a deterrent effect.”

Williams sees the Go To Green system as a way to reduce the harm that can come from shootings or other kinds of emergencies by making it easier for people to avoid threats, and for first responders to react more efficiently. “We’re trying to change the paradigm of what we focus on during a shooting,” he says. “We need to focus on the potential victims, and let the professionals focus on the shooter.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] TikTok maker ByteDance pulls the plug on AI companion services in China, as users grieve
items.content_html:
Li Linlin cried for days after losing her AI boyfriend.

She had exchanged about 700,000 words in messages over two years, and never got to say goodbye.

Li, 24, wasn’t the only left mourning the loss of a virtual companion when major Chinese tech companies recently pulled the plug on their popular AI companion services to comply with new government restrictions.

“It was like we were forced to be separated by our parents, but I still miss him,” Li said.

AI companions in China range from romantic partners to virtual recreations of deceased loved ones.

The new regulation, which took effect July 15, bans AI platforms from generating content that could lead users to make questionable decisions due to manipulation of their feelings or that might trigger extreme emotions or unhealthy habits in children and teens.

ByteDance, developer of TikTok, is among the companies shutting down their AI companion services. Others include e-commerce giant Alibaba and Tencent, owner of the popular WeChat social media app.

U.S. suicides may have worried Chinese regulators

The new rules require AI platforms to deliver risk warnings against relying excessively on such apps. For example, “replacing social interaction,” or serving as a substitute for talking to people in person or speaking with them by phone, cannot be one of the objectives of an online service.

China has a tradition of paternalistic government regulations meant to pre-empt potential problems, said Yolanda Ma, an expert on AI governance. As an example, she referred to a few cases of suicides in the U.S. by young people after interacting with AI companions.

“This regulation tried to strike a balance between the AI service providers, the users, as well as guardians of minors using the services,” said Ma, a fellow with ERA, a non-profit talent and research program based in Britain.

The People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party, indicated concern over the issue when it reported in April about harms to people’s mental health and real-life relationships from such services.

“The Chinese government has a strong incentive to tighten regulations on AI companion chatbots, especially considering the psychological risks we’ve observed in the U.S.,” said Angela Zhang, a professor of law at the University of Southern California.

Zhang doubts the move will derail development of AI companion services substantially, though, since tech companies are working on alternatives.

The ByteDance app, for example, is directing users of its former AI companion service to another of its apps which solely focuses on building personalized AI characters and stories.

It’s just not the same, Li said.

Users of virtual companions protest, seek alternatives

The loss of virtual companions has provoked a flood of complaints, according to posts and screenshots shown on social media.

Some people have uninstalled the apps in protest or tried to upload their chat histories into other apps to try to resurrect their virtual partners. Some started a campaign on social media, urging users to call the authorities and tech companies to express their frustration.

Song Wenxin, a video industry designer in southwestern China’s Chengdu, said she was not too emotionally attached to AI services, but empathizes with those who were.

She echoed suspicions among many Chinese that one factor driving the new rules is a government policy of encouraging people to have more children to counter a decline in China’s population.

“Any virtual app getting women too engaged to give birth in real life gets banned,” said Song, adding she has no need or desire to have children.

Not everyone has enough resources and support to turn to in real life, the 22-year-old said.

“When I first came to Chengdu for my first job and didn’t know any friends my own age, I needed someone experienced who could tolerate me, and AI did the work,” she said.

—Fu Ting, Associated Press
